A.explanation: This is about $1.0 \text{ MW}$, the power needed for the $14\,000 \text{ kg}$ of passengers alone, ignoring the $80\,000 \text{ kg}$ train mass.

B.explanation: This is about $2.8 \text{ MW}$, the useful power to gain gravitational potential energy before allowing for the $40\%$ efficiency.

C.explanation: Total mass $94\,000 \text{ kg}$ gives useful power $mgv\sin30^{\circ} \approx 2.77 \text{ MW}$, and dividing by $0.40$ gives about $6.9 \text{ MW}$ engine power.

D.explanation: This is about $14 \text{ MW}$, obtained if the full weight $mg$ is multiplied by $6.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ with no $\sin30^{\circ}$ factor for the vertical rise.

hints: Add the masses actually being raised: $200 \times 70 \text{ kg}$ for people plus $80\,000 \text{ kg}$ for the train, and note the speed $6.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ is along the $30^{\circ}$ slope.
Useful power for climbing is weight times vertical speed, so multiply by $\sin30^{\circ}$: $P_{useful} = mgv\sin30^{\circ}$ with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
The $2.8 \text{ MW}$ value is only $40\%$ of the engine output, so divide it by $0.40$ to get total engine power in $\text{MW}$.
walkthrough: Find the total mass being lifted: passengers $200 \times 70 = 14\,000 \text{ kg}$, so $m = 80\,000 + 14\,000 = 94\,000 \text{ kg}$.
State the rule for power against gravity at constant speed: $P_{useful} = Fv$, where $F$ is the force along motion balancing the component of weight, $mg\sin30^{\circ}$.
Calculate: $94\,000 \times 9.81 \times 3.0 \approx 2.77 \times 10^6 \text{ W} \approx 2.8 \text{ MW}$ of useful power, with units of $\text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$.
Relate to engine power using efficiency: $P_{engine} \times 0.40 = P_{useful}$, so $P_{engine} = 2.77/0.40 \approx 6.9 \text{ MW}$. This is option C.
